title: The US Just Proposed a 12.5% Tariff on India. The Justification: Forced Labour in the Supply Chain.
excerpt: Section 301 targets 60 economies. India's cotton, aluminium, rice, and fish exports are in the crosshairs. The bilateral trade deal may be the only shield.
body:
The United States has proposed an additional 12.5 per cent tariff on imports from India under a Section 301 investigation, accusing 60 economies of failing to prevent trade in goods linked to forced labour. The proposal, announced by US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on June 3, represents a fresh layer of trade friction even as both countries race to close a bilateral deal by mid-July.

India rejected the allegations outright. The Commerce Ministry said it remains "engaged with the US on the matter as part of Section 301 proceedings" while continuing parallel negotiations on the framework agreement announced in February.

## What Section 301 Actually Is

Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 is a legal mechanism that allows the US government to respond to what it deems unfair foreign trade practices. It has no statutory cap on tariff levels and no expiration date — making it a far more durable tool than the emergency tariffs the Supreme Court struck down in February.

The forced-labour framing is new. The USTR investigated 60 economies covering more than 99 per cent of US imports and concluded that each had failed to impose or effectively enforce a prohibition on importing goods produced with forced labour. India was flagged across multiple sectors: aluminium, cotton, fish, coffee, nickel, palm oil, and rice.

The proposed tariff structure splits targets into two tiers. Canada, the EU, Mexico, Indonesia, Ecuador, and Pakistan face a 10 per cent additional duty. India, China, Japan, South Korea, Brazil, and 48 other economies face the steeper 12.5 per cent rate.

Certain categories are exempt: energy, pharmaceuticals, beef, coffee, and some fruits and vegetables. A special mechanism for textiles and apparel could allow some imports at lower rates.

## The Timing Is Awkward

The Section 301 announcement landed on June 3 — the second day of a three-day US trade delegation visit to New Delhi led by chief negotiator Brendan Lynch. The optics were unusual: American negotiators were in the Indian capital discussing a bilateral trade deal while Washington simultaneously announced an investigation that could impose duties on Indian goods.

Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal, speaking in Visakhapatnam on Friday, appeared unfazed. He said both sides were "fast-moving towards closing all the open ends" of the proposed deal and that the first tranche could be executed by mid-July.

"We had excellent discussions from June 2 to 4 this month," Goyal said. "I expect even a higher-level delegation to be coming to India, probably towards the end of this month."

The initial tranche is expected to give India preferential trade access over competitors — essentially a carve-out that would insulate New Delhi from the worst of the broader tariff regime.

## What It Means for Indian Exporters

The sectors flagged in the investigation — cotton, aluminium, rice, fish, coffee — are significant for Indian exports. Cotton textiles alone account for billions of dollars in annual shipments to the US. Rice exports, already under pressure from production concerns tied to El Niño, could face a double hit if duties are applied.

The aluminium and nickel categories intersect with India's ambitions in critical minerals processing. The government recently announced incentives for lithium and nickel refining, aiming to break China's dominance in the battery supply chain. A 12.5 per cent tariff on processed metals could undercut that strategy before it gains momentum.

For IT services and pharmaceuticals — India's two largest export categories to the US — the impact is limited. Both are excluded from the proposed tariffs.

## The Forced-Labour Question

Trade experts and human rights organisations are sceptical of the administration's framing. Ram Ben Tzion, CEO of shipment-vetting platform Publican, told Reuters the measure "has very little or anything to do with forced labour. It's just a new justification for trade tariffs."

The International Labour Organization estimates 27.6 million people are in forced labour globally, with nearly half in export-related sectors. But the Section 301 investigation does not target specific products made with forced labour. Instead, it targets entire economies for failing to enact import bans — a structural allegation that applies to virtually every trading nation.

India's own forced-labour laws are fragmented. The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act of 1976 prohibits debt bondage, but enforcement is uneven. India has no equivalent of the US Uyghur Forced Labour Prevention Act, which blocks imports from China's Xinjiang region unless importers prove goods were not made with forced labour.

## The Consultation Timeline

The proposed tariffs are not final. Requests for public hearings are due by June 22. Written comments can be submitted until July 6. Public hearings begin July 7. The USTR will consider testimony before issuing a final determination.

That timeline means the tariffs could take effect as early as late July or August — coinciding with the period when the first tranche of the India-US bilateral deal is expected to be signed.

The question is whether the bilateral deal can shield India from Section 301 duties, or whether the two tracks will collide. Indian negotiators have reportedly placed tariff relief from the Section 301 investigation at the top of the agenda during this week's talks. The answer will determine whether India's exporters face one headwind or two.

*Sources: US Trade Representative, Reuters, Bloomberg Law, India Commerce Ministry*
